entries.title: Sky’s playoff hopes officially end in tense loss to Fever
entries.summary: <p>The predictable happened Sunday: With the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> loss to the Fever and the Mystics’ win, the Sky were eliminated from playoff contention.</p><p>Reaching the eighth and final playoff spot remained a goal after the All-Star break, and the Sky have played much better in the second half. They simply had dug themselves too deep a hole.</p><p>Meanwhile, the tension between the Sky and Fever — and around the WNBA — kept simmering.</p><p><b>DiJonai Carrington</b> circled the date of Sunday’s game on social media after she was ejected from the teams’ previous matchup for a flagrant foul on <b>Sophie Cunningham</b>. She also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/10/dijonai-carrington-says-white-privilege-post-goes-beyond-flagrant-foul" >wrote “WHITE PRIVILEGE”</a> on Threads in a since-deleted post.</p><p>There were no ejections this time, but sparks did fly.</p><p>After being called for a foul on <b>Caitlin Clark</b>, Carrington pulled her head back in exaggerated fashion, insinuating Clark had flopped. The two exchanged words. Two possessions later, Clark hit a step-back three-pointer, then had a few more words for Carrington, who finished with seven points on 3-for-11 shooting.</p><p>The game was close until it wasn’t.</p><p>The Sky took a one-point lead into halftime, powered by their bench mob. Rookie <b>Aicha Coulibaly</b> had one of her best games of the season, scoring 12 points on perfect 5-for-5 shooting. <b>Natasha Cloud</b> led the Sky with 16 points, and <b>Azura Stevens</b> added 14.</p><p>But the Sky fell apart in the fourth quarter as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/23/in-a-higher-scoring-league-the-fever-are-one-of-the-best-offenses-ever" >Fever’s offense </a>proved too much. Clark led the way with 34 points, while <b>Kelsey Mitchell</b> added 28.</p><p>Coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> maintained that the Sky still have a lot to play for.</p><p>“I don’t think anybody in the locker room is ready to mail it in," he said. "We all understand we got a job to do. We got an organization and city to continue to play for. We got a lot of young players that still have time to continue to develop. We’re not just playing for the right now, we’re playing for the future too.”</p><h3>Courtside clowns</h3><p>After hitting a big shot in the third quarter, Cloud turned and yelled at former NBA player <b>Enes Freedom</b>, who was sitting courtside in a shirt defining a woman as an “adult female.”</p><p>Freedom recently announced his supposed entry into the WNBA draft, an obvious stunt meant to mock the league and demean transgender people.</p><p>Ever since Cunningham publicly opposed transgender women competing in women’s sports, grifters and provocateurs have used the WNBA to advance their agendas.</p><p>Cloud let Freedom know what she thought of his presence, and teammates had to pull her away.</p><p>Marsh said he told Cloud that the team embraces her as “someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected.”</p><h3>Growing pains</h3><p>After playing the hero against the Valkyries, rookie <b>Sydney Taylor</b> had a tough night against the Fever, shooting 2-for-9. Marsh thought she forced things early but had earned grace.</p><p>“I just told her: Look, you’ve been who you’ve been for this team, and you’re going to continue to be that for a lot longer. You’re going to have a lot more game-winners, and you’re going to have a lot more [crappy] games. That comes with being a future star in this league.”</p>

entries.title: Boy, 15, shot on Lower West Side
entries.summary: <p>A teenage boy was shot in the Lower West Side neighborhood Sunday afternoon, police said.</p><p>The boy, 15, was sitting near a sidewalk in the 1900 block of West Cermak Avenue around 3:30 p.m. when someone in a nearby car fired shots, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The boy was taken to Stroger Hospital, where he was listed in good condition.</p><p>Detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: In a higher-scoring league, the Fever are one of the best offenses ever
entries.summary: <p>In the lead-up to the Bears’ season — have you heard that it’s football season? — coach Ben Johnson set an audacious goal for his offense.</p><p>He doesn’t just want it to be good. He wants it to be one of the best of all time.</p><p>The Fever are already doing that in the WNBA.</p><p>They are averaging 96.2 points per game, on pace to break the record set by the 2023 champion Aces. But Fever coach Stephanie White didn’t enter the season sounding anything like Johnson.</p><p>“I always talk about defense,” she said. “We know we can score, but so can other teams, right?”</p><p>That’s the irony of the Fever: A defensive-minded coach, hired in part to turn around their defense, wound up overseeing one of the greatest offenses ever.</p><p>So in honor of the final <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a>-Fever matchup of the season, in which the Fever rolled to a 113-90 victory, here’s a question with an obvious answer:</p><p>What does it take to build a historically good offense?</p><p>Historically good players.</p><p>So says Sky coach Tyler Marsh, who was an assistant on that 2023 Aces team.</p><p>“They’re loaded, so there’s no surprise,” he said. “They’re extremely talented individually. They run with great pace. They can hurt you in the half court. Steph is a great coach. Put all those things together, it’s no surprise where they are.”</p><p>For all White’s pleading about defense — the Fever rank only 11th in defensive rating — she admits it’s pretty fun to coach a group this loaded.</p><p>The Fever have not one but two MVP candidates: Caitlin Clark, one of the most perceptive passers the league has seen, and Kelsey Mitchell, one of its most unstoppable scorers.</p><p>Ask almost any WNBA player who the toughest cover in the league is the answer tends to be Mitchell. This season, her efficiency has elevated her into historic company. Mitchell is averaging 24.7 points on 50/44/85 shooting splits, numbers comparable to all-time great Diana Taurasi in 2006.</p><p>Asked whether it feels like the Fever are producing a historically good offense, the nine-year veteran said not really.</p><p>“There’s always progress to be made, honestly,” Mitchell said. “People see that it’s been good. Imagine what it could be if you actually cleaned up some things.”</p><p>There's another irony. For all their offensive prowess, the Fever are still frustratingly turnover-prone.</p><p>Cleaning that up would make them even scarier. But whether the fifth-place Fever make a serious championship run will depend more on whether they can defend.</p><p>White is right: They aren’t the only team that can score.</p><p>The third- and fourth-best offenses in WNBA history belong to the 2026 Lynx and Aces.</p><p>“We can’t get caught up in thinking we can outscore everybody,” White said. “We can outscore some people, but we can’t outscore everybody. When you’re trying to accomplish what we’re trying to accomplish, we can’t be lulled into thinking that’s going to be enough.</p><p>The Fever’s record-setting pace isn’t happening in isolation. The WNBA is simply a higher-scoring league in 2026.</p><p>There are plenty of explanations: a greater emphasis on three-pointers, a sharper focus on analytically valuable shots and more free-throw attempts as the game is officiated more tightly.</p><p>The Fever, and Clark in particular, sit at the intersection of it all.</p><p>Clark represents a new kind of point guard: a great playmaker who also takes half her shots from three. Players like Sabrina Ionescu foreshadowed her arrival, but Clark has stretched the combination to its extreme.</p><p>Loaded indeed.</p><p>Before the game, White called Clark and Mitchell two of the most gifted guards in the league. She also did not, as this column nearly did, forget to mention Aliyah Boston, one of the league’s premier post players, who missed the game against the Sky.</p><p>But White always returns to where her heart is:</p><p>“At the end of the day, you’ve got to be able to defend in our sport to be able to compete for championships.”</p>

entries.title: In blowout win, Ian Happ, Pedro Ramirez become fourth Cubs duo to hit grand slams in same game
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Cubs left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> had a chance to join a mighty exclusive baseball fraternity.</p><p>Only 13 players in major-league history have hit two grand slams in the same game, and after Happ banged his first off the foul pole in the third inning Sunday, he strolled to the plate with the bases loaded again in the eighth. He drew a walk instead of becoming the newest member of the club.</p><p>Two batters later, however, infielder <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> shot himself and Happ into the franchise record book by hitting a slam of his own. The duo became the fourth pair of Cubs hitters with grand slams in the same game.</p><p>For the nostalgia buffs out there, the others were <b>Tom Burns</b> and <b>Mal Kittridge</b> on Aug. 16, 1890; <b>Brian Dayett</b> and <b>Keith Moreland</b> on June 3, 1987; and <b>Matt Duffy</b> and <b>Frank Schwindel</b> on Sept. 5, 2021.</p><p>More than geeking out over the feat, however, the Cubs were more focused on the offensive day as a whole. They throttled the Mariners 19-2, putting the same kind of hurt on them the Brewers did with a 22-0 rout Tuesday.</p><p>Happ’s slam came after three consecutive two-out walks against Mariners starter <b>Bryce Miller</b>, who walked seven after coming in with only one game with more than four walks in his big-league career.</p><p>It was an explosive way to salvage a victory in the series after losing in walk-off fashion Friday and Saturday.</p><p>‘‘We did a really good job the first couple of games of this series and scored [five runs Friday and four Saturday], but we had opportunities to score more,’’ Happ said. ‘‘When we have days like that, it feels like one of these is coming. That’s how good the offense has been this year.’’</p><p>Despite being a prime target of frustrated fans because of poorer-than-usual production, particularly against left-handed pitching, Happ quietly has had a nice couple of weeks, hitting .298 with a .389 on-base percentage, four homers, nine RBI and nine runs scored in his last 14 games.</p><h3>Civale steps up</h3><p>Left-hander <b>Shota Imanaga</b> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/23/cubs-mariners-brewers-nl-central-standings-shota-imanaga-stats-starting-rotation-playoffs" target="_blank" >got a quick hook</a> after struggling early and was lifted after the first two Mariners reached base in the third.</p><p>After the game, the Cubs were ecstatic about the relief performance they got from right-hander <b>Aaron Civale</b> — four scoreless innings of one-hit ball — who quietly has excelled out of the bullpen since joining the team last month.</p><p>In nine appearances, Civale has a 1.80 ERA and has eaten innings as one of the team’s several long relievers, a stockpile that allowed manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> to be confident in removing Imanaga in what was then a three-run game with 6½ innings to play.</p><p>‘‘It’s pounding the strike zone; that’s what he’s done so good in the bullpen,’’ Counsell said of Civale. ‘‘There’s no walks, so you’ve got to get a hit to get on base against him. He’s done a fabulous job of that. . . . He’s been really effective in that role.”</p><h3>See you in Williamsport</h3><p>MLB announced the Cubs will take on the Blue Jays in the Little League Classic on Aug. 19 next season in Williamsport, Pennsylvania.</p><p>The game has been held every year since 2017 — except in 2020 because of COVID — in connection with the Little League World Series and offers young players a chance to interact with major-league stars.</p>

entries.title: Cubs avoid sweep, but what’s concern level with NL Central gap widening, Shota Imanaga getting quick hook?
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> can be happy they didn’t get swept out of the Pacific Northwest by a sub-.500 Mariners team after winning with a 19-2 rout Sunday.</p><p>But with the final month of the regular season approaching, the Cubs are watching the National League Central-leading Brewers get further away in the standings, all while one of the key pieces to their pitching puzzle is fresh off the shortest outing of his major-league career.</p><p>After recently shrinking the Brewers’ lead in the division to three games, the smallest it had been since May, the Cubs entered Sunday behind by seven games, the largest deficit they had faced in weeks. That fell to six with the Brewers’ loss to the Braves.</p><p>All the while, the Phillies — with former Cubs slugger Kyle Schwarber hitting dramatic walk-off home runs — and Padres are hot on their heels in a tightening wild-card race.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">WALK-OFF SCHWARBOMB OVER THE BATTER'S EYE!!!!!! <a href="https://t.co/O9YgxPWSac">pic.twitter.com/O9YgxPWSac</a></p>— Philadelphia Phillies (@Phillies) <a href="https://x.com/Phillies/status/2091621299013505460?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 23, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The sky might be falling for panicky standings-watchers across the North Side. Rest assured, however, that’s not what’s happening in the Cubs’ clubhouse.</p><p>‘‘We have to win baseball games,’’ manager Craig Counsell said before the game Sunday. ‘‘Do you know what the other teams around you are doing? Of course, you do. But we have to win games. And when you don’t really control what the other teams do, it’s [about] your team and you winning games. . . .</p><p></p><p>‘‘I’m not sure what me looking and worrying about that stuff will do for the Cubs. You see the score, you say, ‘Oh, they won. OK, great.’ ’’</p><p></p><p>The Cubs’ shot at the Brewers will come soon enough, with seven games still to play against them.</p><p></p><p>‘‘Seasons always come down to the last week,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘The thing I always think about, the standings go up and down. And, obviously, you’d love to make it as easy as you can on yourself. But then you’re always in the last 10 days of the season. That’s how it happens. That’s how it works.’’</p><p></p><p>But other questions are popping up, such as whom the Cubs will be able to count on in those critical games against the Brewers.</p><p></p><p>They opted to keep left-hander Shota Imanaga from starting against the Brewers in the last game they played in 2025, the decisive fifth game of the NL Division Series. He had limped into the playoffs with a 6.51 ERA and 10 home runs allowed in five September starts and had given up six runs and three homers in two postseason outings.</p><p></p><p>Imanaga has endured a bit of a bumpy stretch lately, and few of his games as a big-leaguer have been bumpier than the one Sunday. He got only six outs in the shortest outing of his career.</p><p></p><p>Imanaga allowed only a couple runs but put plenty of runners on base, surrendering five hits, walking two and hitting a batter as the pitches piled up in a hurry. One of the hits was a leadoff homer by Randy Arozarena, the 30th long ball Imanaga has given up this season, one shy of the major-league lead.</p><p></p><p>‘‘He was having a bad day,’’ Counsell said after the game. ‘‘Frankly, keeping it to two [runs] through two innings was pretty good. . . . He was struggling today, and you could tell. The misses were far bigger than normal. Velocity was down a little bit from the beginning.’’</p><p></p><p>Though Counsell and the Cubs continue to rave about Imanaga’s work in general, he has a 6.39 ERA with five homers allowed in his last three starts.</p><p></p><p>Time to panic? Not yet. There’s a lot of opportunity for Imanaga to straighten things out before the most important games of the season. But his recent struggles can’t help but bring to mind how things ended last season.</p><p></p><p>‘‘As a starter, you want to keep the team in the game; today, I couldn’t,’’ Imanaga said through an interpreter. ‘‘Next start . . . [I need to] keep us in the game, stay tenacious and help the team.’’</p>

entries.title: School is back in session for CPS students after summer of budget angst
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools students head back to school Monday after a summer in which layoffs and last-minute budget changes made it challenging for schools to staff up for the first day.</p><p>Many principals had planned to start the 2026-27 school year with fewer staff, but then the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>school board overhauled the budget</u></a>, hoping to reverse many planned layoffs.</p><p>That won’t be enough to add back all the lost positions. But district officials say they’re <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/08/22/things-to-watch-as-new-cps-school-year-starts-from-classroom-cuts-to-enrollment-counts" target="_blank" ><u>now in the process of bringing back staff</u></a> and placing them in schools.</p><p>There’s positives, too. District officials point to the addition of special education staff to support the rising number of CPS students with disabilities, and the expansion of dual language and world language programs that help students learn a language other than English.</p><p>And even with the staffing changes, the district has a low teacher vacancy rate, which likely means many laid-off teachers found new jobs within CPS.</p><p>There’s lots of <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/08/22/things-to-watch-as-new-cps-school-year-starts-from-classroom-cuts-to-enrollment-counts" target="_blank" ><u>other issues to watch this year</u></a>, too, including whether the state or city will come through with the extra revenue that CPS is counting on, and how a fully elected school board will shape the direction of the district.</p><p>We’ll be updating this story throughout the day as we check in with students, parents, educators and Supt. Macquline King, who’s set to ring in the start of the school year at Leland Elementary School in Austin this morning.</p>

ancestors. </p><p>My family’s Chicago-based Polish roots run deep, particularly in Pilsen, where many <a class="Link" href="https://www.thepilsenalliance.org/our-history-1" target="_blank" ><u>Polish Our ties to Pilsen — not too far from Bridgeport — is the reason my mother’s side cheers for the White Sox.</p><p>My grandmother’s father moved from Poland to the United States when he was just 6. His parents — my great-great-grandparents — were born in Poland and worked in the U.S. for a year before the rest of the family was able to join them in Chicago.</p><p>My great-grandparents ended up buying a six-flat in Pilsen. The building's units were always abuzz, primarily filled with relatives. It's the site where my grandmother was born and raised. It remained home to my great-grandmother until she died.</p><p>My family members say I have an awful memory. I might. But that doesn't stop the flood of recollections I have of that cozy six-flat on 22nd Place.</p><p>My mind can't erase the wide steps leading up to the building, creating the perfect stoop where me, my siblings and cousins caused many commotions.</p><p>I also can't forget, years later, working up a sweat as some of us hauled boxes out of my great-grandmother’s attic and down the building's narrow stairs after she died.</p><p>I recently asked my grandmother why she thinks my great-grandmother and much of her family ended up in Pilsen. She wasn’t sure. I'm thinking they simply gravitated to where others shared their language and culture.</p><p>My maternal grandmother’s family, like many of overwhelming <a class="Link" href="https://www.state.gov/reports/2022-report-on-international-religious-freedom/poland" target="_blank" ><u>majority</u></a> Chicago-area Catholic Poles, frequented St. Adalbert and St. Paul churches in Pilsen.</p><p>“St. Adalbert, in my area, was the biggest one,” my grandmother told me.</p><p>My great-grandmother and her siblings were all married at St. Adalbert Church. Many of them remain together today resting at St. Adalbert Cemetery, across from the former White Eagle, where my memories were recently triggered.</p><p>I grew up in Oswego and went to college in Ohio. My first job out of school was based in Cincinnati. But I returned. Moving to Chicago to work at the Sun-Times has given me even more appreciation for this city, its people and my family's history.</p><p>When I covered the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/06/17/st-adalbert-landmark-status-zoning-committee-unexpected-change" target="_blank" ><u>landmarking</u></a> of St. Adalbert Church last year, I chatted with my grandmother on the phone. Now, whenever I’m walking through Pilsen with friends and spot the church’s soaring towers, I have stories to tell.</p><p>Writing about the the housing project that is being built on the former White Eagle site sparked more curiosity in me — not just as a reporter but as a Chicagoan whose family is one of many tied to the property.</p><p>As the Sun-Times’ development reporter, I’m lucky to travel to all parts of the city to see new buildings go up, and, sometimes, old ones come down. But the best stories I write are the articles my grandmother reads.</p><p>After reading the print underneath my byline, she often gives me a call, and I get to learn something new.</p><p><i>Abby Miller is a reporter for the Sun-Times. </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4c0000" name="module-4c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: White Sox legend Tommy John deserved a Chicago-style send-off
entries.summary: <p>When former White Sox pitcher Tommy John died over a week ago, the Sun-Times, unfortunately, ran an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/16/tommy-john-namesake-for-a-pioneering-elbow-surgery-that-saved-his-career-dead-at-83" target="_blank" >obituary by the Associated Press</a> instead of having a staffer write about him. To add insult to injury, the photo accompanying the story in print was a snapshot of Tommy as a Dodger instead of as a Sox player.</p><p>The AP article rightfully touches on Tommy John surgery, a path-breaking procedure named after the operation Tommy underwent in 1974 that replaced his torn elbow ligament with a tendon from his right forearm. The story mostly focuses on Tommy's time with the Los Angeles Dodgers and the New York Yankees, giving short shrift to his stints with the Sox, Cleveland Indians, California Angels and Oakland Athletics.</p><p>What can you expect from national writers who don't bother with the Midwest and smaller cites?</p><p>Here is Chicago perspective the Sun-Times could have captured:</p><p>When Cleveland traded Tommy to the Sox in 1965, the Sox also got <a class="Link" href="https://www.baseball-almanac.com/players/trades.php?p=ageeto01" target="_blank" >Tommie Agee</a>, one of the few good hitters the Sox had for a period. With the Sox, Tommy tied or led the majors in shutouts in 1966 and 1967. Tommy was considered the ace of the Sox’s pitching staff in 1966 and 1970. With Tommy and other great pitchers on the mound, the 1967 White Sox nearly won the pennant and led the American League for most of that season. In 1968, while on the Sox, Tommy had a microscopic 1.98 ERA and made the All-Star team.</p><p>The Sox’s trading of Tommy to the Dodgers before the 1972 season brought the Sox the great Dick Allen, who saved the franchise (the Sox were in danger of relocating a few years later) and nearly slugged the Sox into the playoffs. Without Tommy, the Sox never would have gotten Allen, and the Sox could have ended up in Seattle or Denver.</p><p>Let's not forget who Tommy John was to many of us Chicagoans: A White Sox star of the mid-1960s and early 1970s.</p><p>RIP, Tommy.</p><p><i>William S. Bike, Clearing</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Be fair by approving<b> </b>Protecting Renters Ordinance</h3><h3></h3><p>In recent weeks, some Chicago City Council members have advanced the Fair and Accountable Illinois Rental, or FAIR, ordinance as an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/27/renters-protection-ordinances-mayor-brandon-johnson-aldermanic-opponents-dueling-versions-chicago-city-council" >alternative </a>to Mayor Brandon Johnson's proposed Protecting Renters Ordinance, or PRO, supported by housing justice advocates, including the Metropolitan Tenants Organization.</p><p>It should be noted the FAIR ordinance doesn't live by its name. FAIR rolls back existing law by vastly expanding landlord exemptions from the Residential Landlord Tenant Ordinance, weakening tenant protections and creating an opportunistic environment for the landlord lobby. FAIR also falls short by completely removing the ordinance's central housing stability measure: "<a class="Link" href="https://www.justcausechicago.org/" target="_blank" >just cause</a>" provisions, which would protect tenants from a landlord’s arbitrary decision not to renew a lease, while providing relocation assistance to those displaced through no fault of their own.</p><p>At the Metropolitan Tenants Organization, we see the impacts of no-fault displacement and housing instability every day through our work with city-based tenants. These experiences are exactly why we support PRO’s just cause and relocation assistance provisions. Today, a Chicago tenant who pays rent on time and complies with their lease may still lose their home simply because a landlord declines to renew their lease, for any reason or no reason.</p><p>Decades of <a class="Link" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20200710010146id_/https://nlihc.org/sites/default/files/DesmondKimbro_Evictions_Fallout_SF2015.pdf" target="_blank" >research </a>demonstrates that stable housing is associated with better educational outcomes, improved physical and mental health, stronger neighborhood cohesion and greater economic opportunity. This is not surprising, as housing provides far more than shelter. It anchors children to schools, connects workers to jobs, sustains neighborhood relationships, and provides the stability households need to plan for the future.</p><p>Several states and over 20 of the nation’s largest cities have adopted some form of just cause provisions because they recognize housing stability as a legitimate public interest. Contrary to opponents’ claims, just cause and relocation assistance are <a class="Link" href="https://www.publicgoodpolicy.org/just-cause" target="_blank" >not correlated</a> with faster rent growth or less development.</p><p>Tenant protections are not the drivers of decreasing affordability — they are vital interventions in a market that is otherwise easily exploited by bad actors. PRO will improve protections. FAIR will take them away and roll back years of progress.</p><p>The City Council has an opportunity to protect and stabilize tenants rights, and we urge them to move forward and strengthen tenant protections by supporting PRO, not backward, by rolling them back with FAIR.</p><p><i>Cassie Armea-Warren, deputy director, Metropolitan Tenants Organization</i></p><h3></h3><h3>Don’t <b>dismiss</b> USS Abraham Lincoln claims </h3><p>The reports about conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln should concern every American.</p><p>Sailors, Marines and their families have <a class="Link" href="https://www.denver7.com/news/local-news/colorado-congressman-demands-answers-on-uss-abraham-lincoln-conditions-after-260-day-deployment" target="_blank" >described</a> broken toilets, plumbing problems, shortages of food and hygiene supplies, and serious mental health concerns after an extraordinarily long deployment. There are even <a class="Link" href="https://thenationaldesk.com/news/americas-news-now/uss-abraham-lincoln-deployment-hits-ninth-month-setting-modern-record-at-sea" target="_blank" >reports</a> of sailors attempting to go overboard.</p><p>Yet, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dismisses these reports as <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/policy/defense/6028091-pete-hegseth-uss-abraham-lincoln-conditions-middle-east/" target="_blank" >“completely misrepresented.”</a> That response is difficult to accept when multiple families, military reporters and members of Congress are raising similar concerns.</p><p>Maybe every allegation isn’t 100% accurate, but instead of dismissing them, Hegseth should demand an independent investigation and let the facts speak for themselves.</p><p>Our sailors and Marines risk their lives for this country. They deserve decent living conditions, honest leadership and, above all, to be heard.</p><p>Shouldn’t these sailors and Marines be afforded the same conditions as those enjoyed by convicted child sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell at her <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/09/03/nx-s1-5519224/ghislaine-maxwell-prison-texas-epstein" target="_blank" >country club prison in Texas</a>?</p><p><i>Tom Scorby, St. Charles</i></p><h3>Trump’s renovation ruse </h3><p>Good to know that our prez found the time last week to give some <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/19/trump-white-house-renovations" target="_blank" >folks a guided tour</a> of the "improvements" he's making to our White House and its grounds.</p><p>He needs to take an occasional break from his ongoing negotiations with Iran, Oman, Benjamin Netanyahu, Hamas, Cuba, Greenland, that NATO gang and our pesky northern neighbors.</p><p><i>Dan McGuire, Bensenville</i></p>

entries.title: With Bears desperate for instant impact, rookie S Dillon Thieneman in 'very good spot'
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — One of the best things <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ defense has going for it amid a challenging training camp is the rapid progress of rookie safety Dillon Thieneman. They need him to make an instant impact, especially with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/11/bears-s-coby-bryant-undergoes-knee-surgery-now-out-until-at-least-december" >Coby Bryant possibly out for the season</a>, and he’s becoming a versatile weapon in their secondary.</p><p>There’s a lot of pressure on him, but he seems up for it. Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has been tailoring his role at strong safety, playing him up in the box against the run and sticking him on tight ends in pass coverage, whether that’s Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet in normal practices, or the Bengals’ Mike Gesicki in the recent joint practice in Cincinnati.</p><p>“I’m at a very good spot,” Thieneman told the Sun-Times. “As we add stuff each week and do stuff for specific opponents, that might change, but that comes along with more practices. Right now, with the playbook, I feel very comfortable.</p><p>“I’m feeling more and more confident as I go. Going against some of the better tight ends has really helped me.”</p><p>Thieneman played 14 snaps on defense and two on special teams Saturday in the Bears’ 27-9 preseason loss to the Bengals. He got 14 plays defensively the week before against the Browns, too.</p><p>The best work he gets in pass coverage, though, comes against Loveland. He’s a monster at 6-foot-6, 241 pounds with great speed and has been a constant playmaker in training camp. In one series against the Bengals on Saturday, he broke free for what could’ve been a 27-yard touchdown, but quarterback Caleb Williams overthrew him.</p><p>“You’ve got to be on your Ps and Qs, dialed in on everything and ready to ball out,” Thieneman said of covering Loveland. “He’s a great player, very athletic, fast, long arms, so even if you’re in the right position, he still might make a great play. It just helps you get better and better.”</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Dad Asks a Lot of Low-Income Live-at-Home Son
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My middle-aged son is on the autism spectrum and has recently come back home to live with us. He left home at 19 and has always had roommates. We didn't realize that he had autism until about a year ago.</p><p>We like having him here but are having a difficult time adjusting. My son has agreed to help with bills and contribute toward groceries, but my husband thinks we should split all expenses three ways equally. My son works in the food service industry and earns a low wage, even though he puts in 32 to 34 hours a week. He eats at work most of the time and at home only twice a week. I'm retired and live on a small Social Security check. My husband makes more than twice what my son and I make.</p><p>I think we should contribute based on our income, and I feel that my son and I should contribute 20% each toward food and other bills. Every time I try to discuss this with my husband, he gets angry and accuses me of taking advantage of him. I'm hoping we can get this resolved and move on. — <i>DESPERATE MOM</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOM:</b> I assume you want your son to stay with you for the long term; does your husband feel the same? Is it possible he's being difficult about money so your son will move out again?</p><p>The phrase "on the autism spectrum" covers a wide range of needs, so I'm not in a position to weigh in on what you should expect of your son. A licensed family counselor who specializes in autism may be able to help you and your husband understand how much your son is capable of contributing.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My fiance, "Dustin," and I have been a couple for five years. We live together and are fairly happy. The problem is his gaming habits. At first, it wasn't an issue because I also play the occasional video game. Since moving into our own place, I've noticed Dustin has started spending a tremendous amount of time on these video games. From the time he wakes up around 1 p.m. until right after he gets off work around 10 p.m., he'll log on and play for hours. Most nights he doesn't come to bed until 5 a.m.!</p><p>With all his free time, he doesn't help clean or cook, and I get none of his attention. I'm not sure where I go from here. I have spoken to him about this habit, but he doesn't see any issue because he grew up constantly playing games. I need some guidance on this issue because it's driving a wedge in our relationship. — <i>GAME OVER IN NORTH CAROLINA</i></p><p><b>DEAR GAME OVER:</b> Dustin doesn't see any issue with the status quo because it isn't a problem — for him. He's got a pretty good deal. You do the cooking and the cleaning and contribute to half the expenses, but you're not even getting companionship.</p><p>Tell your fiance you need more from him because this isn't what you signed up for when you moved in together. Offer him the option of couples counseling so your issues can be mediated. If he isn't willing and this doesn't resolve the problem, then cut your losses and move out unless you want to spend the rest of your life as a "gaming widow."</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: A member of Rosemont's powerful Stephens family who sits on the Triton College board arrested on drug charges
entries.summary: <p>Mark Stephens — a son of late Rosemont Mayor Donald E. Stephens, a brother of current Mayor Bradley Stephens and the chairman of the Triton College board — was arrested recently on drug charges during a traffic stop in the far northwest suburbs.</p><p>Mark Stephens, 67, was charged with unlawful possession of a controlled substance after he was seen dropping an unmarked prescription bottle under his car while getting out of the vehicle after being pulled over for speeding, according to Harvard police.</p><p>The bottle contained a substance that later tested positive for cocaine, police say.</p><p>“During the traffic stop, officers detected the odor of unburnt cannabis coming from the vehicle,” police said in a statement. “Officers asked the driver ... if there was cannabis inside the vehicle. Stephens subsequently handed officers an open container of cannabis.”</p><p>Mark Stephens was also charged with unlawful possession of cannabis by a driver, and he was cited for speeding.</p><p>Mark Stephens is a resident of Rosemont, a tiny but politically influential near northwest suburb in the shadow of O’Hare Airport. He couldn’t be reached for comment.</p><p>A spokesman for Bradley Stephens, who also serves as a state legislator, says: “The mayor is aware of the situation, that his brother Mark was arrested,” and “it’s a personal matter.”</p><p>“Obviously, the mayor feels it’s unfortunate, and he hopes Mark gets any help that’s needed,” the spokesman says. “He wishes him well in that regard.”</p><p>Rosemont was founded in the 1950s by Donald E. entries.title: Rare black fox, whose coloration is the result of a genetic quirk, makes home in north suburban Northbrook
entries.summary: <p>Most red foxes are — predictably, given the name of the breed — reddish in color, skewing orange.</p><p>But in Northbrook, an unusual variant of red fox has been slinking about: One with fur that’s almost all black, coloration wildlife experts say is quite rare and the result of a genetic quirk.</p><p>Believed to be a male of about 15 pounds, it’s been seen in a number of places in the northern suburb over the last year or two, according to the village’s animal control officer, Gina Manski.</p><p>“I just got a picture a couple days ago” of the animal, Manski said, courtesy of a police officer who snapped a shot and sent it her way.</p><p>“I get a ton of photos of him” from locals, she said. “Either they don’t know what it is, or it’s like, ‘Look at this cool fox!’”</p><p>She’s seen it in person just once, last year.</p><p>“He was limping on a back leg,” Manski said, though the creature was nonetheless able to hop a five-foot chain-link fence and dart away.</p><p>The limp is now gone, so the fox has apparently recovered from whatever injury it had.</p><p>Foxes like this are called “melanistic” because they have elevated levels of melanin that determines pigmentation, experts say.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ce0000" entries.title: Total of Cook County property taxes billed goes up for the 32nd consecutive year, treasurer's office says
entries.summary: <p>With Cook County’s 2025 property tax bills set to go out by the end of the month, a new <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountytreasurer.com/pdfs/taxbillanalysisandstatistics/taxyear2025analysisenglishversion.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>report</u></a> from county Treasurer Maria Pappas’ office finds the total amount of property taxes billed has risen for the 32nd consecutive year.</p><p></p><p>Commercial property values increased by 0.2%, not nearly enough to offset a rise in property values for homeowners, whose bills <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/30/property-taxes-cook-county-treasurer-study" target="_blank" ><u>continued to outpace the 2.7% inflation</u></a> rate. The tax levy increased by nearly 4% last year.</p><p>It’s a continuation of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/03/07/property-taxes-loop-pandemic-christopher-berry-pat-quinn-joseph-schwieterman-joseph-ferguson-farzin-parang" target="_blank" ><u>yearslong trend of the property tax burden shifting</u></a> from downtown to the city’s neighborhoods, and even suburban residential properties. The COVID-19 pandemic reduced occupancy in many downtown buildings, leading to dips in property values and businesses’ tax bills dropping nearly 20%. In the meantime, residential bills increased more than 16% in the 2021 to 2023 reassessment cycle — and hundreds of thousands of homeowners <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/05/cook-county-treasurer-maria-pappas-report-property-tax-appeals" target="_blank" ><u>saw even larger increases</u></a>.</p><p>The share of the tax burden taken on by residential property owners, who were on the hook for about 58% of the tax burden in 2025, has stayed relatively the same since the last round of bills. But residential properties countywide gained 6.84% in value, increasing their tax bills by 5.34%, or a collective $600 million, between 2024 and 2025. </p><p>Chicago’s residential properties bore 20% of the total increase, about $120 million. It comes after Black neighborhoods on the South and West sides <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/11/17/cook-county-property-taxes-analysis-treasurer-maria-pappas-downtown-south-west-sides" target="_blank" ><u>saw the sharpest increases</u></a> in their 2024 tax bills.</p><p>Bridgeport and Logan Square both saw median tax bill increases of $274 each in 2025, while West Town and North Center saw median increases over $350.</p><p>But the largest median tax bill increases proportionally were seen in Douglas, which saw tax bills jump 6.23%. Uptown and Englewood followed with 5.48% and 5.21% increases respectively.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/05/cook-county-treasurer-maria-pappas-report-property-tax-appeals" >‘Broken’ tax appeals system put extra $2 billion on Cook County homeowners, treasurer says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/11/17/cook-county-property-taxes-analysis-treasurer-maria-pappas-downtown-south-west-sides" >Black neighborhoods hit hardest with Cook County property tax bill increase, analysis finds</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/05/south-and-west-side-clergy-call-for-relief-from-sinful-property-tax-spikes" >South and West side clergy seek relief from ‘sinful’ property tax spikes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Homes in the north suburbs — which were reassessed for the 2025 cycle — saw the largest spike, nearly 10%, or about a $360 million increase. The south and west suburbs are up for reassessment for the 2026 cycle, and the city for 2027.</p><p>Unincorporated New Trier Township saw the median tax bill increase 27.8%, a jump of more than $7,800. Prospect Heights and Melrose Park each saw nearly 21% increases in their bills as well, for a median increase of more than $1,200.</p><p>Businesses in the north suburbs got hit hard as well, with 20% to 30% median bill increases in unincorporated areas of Niles, Wheeling and Norwood Park townships.</p><p>South suburban University Park got some relief, with a median decrease of nearly 30% on 2025 tax bills, while Ford Heights bills dropped 8%.</p><p>Property tax bills were set to be sent out by Aug. 31 after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/06/09/cook-county-property-tax-bills-delay-preckwinkle" target="_blank" ><u>a delay from July</u></a>, with payments due Oct. 1. That's shorter than last year’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/07/cook-county-property-tax-bills-due-dec-15-after-several-months-delay" target="_blank" ><u>four-month delay</u></a> due to a computer issue. The postponement had impacts downstream, as Chicago Public Schools had to pay <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/12/19/property-tax-payment-delay-costs-chicago-public-schools-almost-a-quarter-million-dollars-a-day" target="_blank" ><u>$220,000 in interest per day on short-term loans</u></a> it took out to make payroll last year.</p><p>Pre-filing is already open for 2026 tax bills, and the Cook County Board of Review has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/19/cook-county-board-of-review-urges-residents-to-start-on-appeals-for-2026-tax-bills-after-recent-storm-damage" target="_blank" ><u>urged residents to start the appeals process</u></a>, especially if their property has been damaged by recent waves of storms.</p><p>The gap between the number of wealthy real estate owners and low-income homeowners who appeal their property value assessments has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/05/cook-county-treasurer-maria-pappas-report-property-tax-appeals" target="_blank" ><u>partially blamed by the treasurer’s office</u></a> for why residential property tax bills for lower income households have risen in recent years.</p><p>The treasurer’s office previously blamed Cook County’s “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/05/cook-county-treasurer-maria-pappas-report-property-tax-appeals" target="_blank" ><u>broken system</u></a>” of property tax appeals, which often gives breaks to business owners and wealthy white homeowners who more frequently appeal than low- income homeowners, who became saddled with nearly $2 billion of tax burden because of it.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li entries.title: Prosecutors expected to offer new deal to woman accused of killing boyfriend as trial kicks off
entries.summary: <p>On the eve of Keshia Golden’s trial for fatally stabbing her child’s father, prosecutors are expected to offer a new plea deal for significantly reduced charges and no time behind bars.</p><p>Golden, now 37, says she was acting in self-defense when she stabbed Calvin Sidney at their baby shower almost four years ago.</p><p>Since then, Golden’s lawyers and advocates have been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/02/24/chicago-crime-keshia-golden-domestic-violence-abuse-murder" target="_blank" ><u>urging the Cook County state’s attorney’s office to drop all charges.</u></a> Prosecutors previously offered Golden a chance to plead guilty to lesser charges of second-degree murder in exchange for two years of probation, but her lawyers said <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/03/chicago-keshia-golden-crime-domestic-violence-murder-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" ><u>the conviction would follow her for life.</u></a></p><p>Now, with trial set to begin Monday, prosecutors are expected to present a new deal — plead guilty to involuntary manslaughter and get two years of probation, according to sources familiar with the case. Unlike second-degree murder, an involuntary manslaughter conviction wouldn’t require Golden to register as a violent offender, sources said. Golden’s will formally be offered the deal during a hearing Monday before Judge Steven Watkins, according to the public defenders office.</p><p>Golden and Sidney had just finished hosting a shower for their first child on Oct. 22, 2022, when he slammed her into a kitchen counter and a fridge, according to her lawyers. Golden was eight months pregnant at the time. A relative tried to separate the pair, but Sidney wouldn’t relent, her lawyers said. Golden grabbed a knife and stabbed Sidney’s leg, striking his femoral artery. He later died at Mount Sinai Hospital, officials said.</p><p>“After the stab, I just ran out of the house,” Golden previously told the Sun-Times. “I wasn’t thinking clearly. I just wanted him to stop, basically. I didn’t know that it hit an artery."</p><p>A Cook County judge initially set <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/10/30/23429205/calvin-sydney-dead-pregnant-woman-charged-murder-father-keshia-golden-domestic-violence" target="_blank" ><u>Golden’s bond at $2 million.</u></a> Julie Koehler, deputy chief of the public defender’s homicide task force, rallied anti-domestic violence and community organizations to raise awareness and the money needed to get Golden out of jail. A week later, a different Cook County judge reduced her bail to $50,000, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/11/4/23441087/pregnant-woman-murder-charge-community-group-provides-bond-keshia-golden" target="_blank" ><u>requiring her to pay $5,000 to get out. </u></a>Once she was released, she was able to give birth and raise her now 3-year-old daughter, Ky’liyah.</p><p>For almost four years, Golden has checked in daily with pretrial services and attended all her hearings, the public defenders office said.</p><p>Last month, a jury found Vanessa Sanders not guilty of all charges in a similar case. Sanders was also a pregnant mother charged with murder for allegedly stabbing an abusive partner.</p>

entries.title: Thousands in northwest Indiana still don't have power after storms. Here's what to know.
entries.summary: <p>Northwest Indiana residents continue suffering after back-to-back storms devastated the state earlier this month. </p><p>Winds of nearly 100 miles an hour and torrential downpours knocked down trees into people's homes and driveways and flooded basements and roads. Seven people died across Indiana. The storms caused widespread power outages in much of the state. </p><p>While power has been restored for over 300,000 Hoosiers, many residents are still without power. Gary, one of Indiana's hardest-hit cities, had the most customers in the state waiting for power to return, according to the NIPSCO, northwest Indiana's electric utility company.</p><p>As of Monday morning, 97% of NIPSCO customers who had lost power had their service restored. In Gary, about 8,400 customers remained without power.</p><p>Here's what to know about what happened in northwest Indiana and the relief efforts underway. </p><h3>When will northwest Indiana cities get their power back? </h3><p>NIPSCO reported that more than 60% of its customers — roughly 370,000 — lost power during the Aug. 11 storm and subsequent days of severe weather. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nipsco.com/outages/power-outages" target="_blank" ></a> </p><p> Gary and Portage residents are expected to have to wait till Tuesday for their power to return — two weeks after the Aug. 11 storm. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nipsco.com/outages/power-outages" target="_blank" >Here’s the full list</a> of towns still waiting on power.</p><h3>Why is it taking so long? </h3><p>Part of why it’s taking longer to restore power is the city suffered the most “extensive and complex damage” from the storm, mainly because of the 99 mph winds that tore through northwest The worst was caused by mature large trees crashing onto their properties.</p><p>Crews of linemen are repairing downed power lines and rebuilding destroyed electrical systems. That includes 335 damaged poles that need to be repaired or replaced and 27 outages at substations that need to be fixed before power can be restored.</p><h3>Why did ComEd restore power faster for the south suburbs?</h3><p>The same storm system that hit Indiana also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" target="_blank" >caused seven tornadoes</a> in Chicago's south suburbs. Soon after the storm, ComEd was able to restore power for the vast majority of its customers.</p><p>Melody Birmingham, the group utilities president at NiSource, NIPSCO’s parent company, tried to explain Wednesday why it's taken the utility longer to restore power compared to ComEd. ComEd has four million customers, compared to NIPSCO's 500,000. That means the utility has a much larger staff and is better equipped to respond to outages faster.</p><h3>Are schools still closed? </h3><p>The damage caused by the storms caused many school districts to close schools until power is restored and debris is cleared.</p><p>Gary's schools have been closed all week. As of Aug. 20, <a class="Link" href="https://www.garycsc.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >Gary Community School Corporation</a> was still waiting for power to return to all of the city's schools. The school district, which is posting <a class="Link" href="https://www.garycsc.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >regular updates on its website</a>, has not said if schools will reopen next week. </p><p>In a note posted to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.hobart.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >School City of Hobart’s website</a>, Supt. Peggy Buffington said she anticipates schools opening on Monday. </p><h3>How have businesses been impacted? </h3><p>Many restaurants, gas stations, grocery stores, banks and small businesses across northwest Indiana were also still without power. Many businesses remain closed, while others are able to partially operate. </p><p>Gary was Chamber of Commerce president Charles Hughes said he does not have a timeline for when businesses will have power restored because NIPSCO is prioritizing hospitals and homes.</p><h3>What resources are available? </h3><p>Crews from FEMA and the Indiana Department of Homeland Security are assessing the damage across the state.</p><p>Indiana Gov. Mike Braun has activated <a class="Link" href="https://www.in.gov/dhs/emergency-management-and-preparedness/august-2026-disaster" target="_blank" >the state’s disaster relief fund</a>. People can <a class="Link" href="https://app.smartsheet.com/b/form/01a019f5a4457f0495bbef680cff9c75" target="_blank" >apply online for relief funds</a>. Immediate emergency grants are capped at $5,000. </p><p>Several community groups are also providing resources and shelter. The YWCA, 150 W. 15th Ave., is offering round-the-clock shelter, warm meals and charging stations. The Monroe Center, 4101 Washington St., is offering emergency shelter to residents whose homes were impacted. Family Life Community Center, 565 Massachusetts St., is distributing hot meals and groceries.</p><p>Capital B Gary has compiled this <a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/northwest-indiana-storm-relief-resources/" target="_blank" >list of resources</a> for those in need of help, including where to get hot meals, power for their devices and emergency shelter.</p>

entries.title: Woman dies after being pulled from Lake Michigan on South Side
entries.summary: <p>A woman died after being pulled from Lake Michigan Sunday morning on the South Side. </p><p>The woman was pulled from the water around 10:15 a.m. in the 4500 block of South Lake Shore Drive, Chicago police said. </p><p>She was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where she was pronounced dead, police said. entries.title: Jarrett Payton-David Haugh pairing on The Score's morning show is evidence of dried-up pipeline
entries.summary: <p>A newspaper guy and a TV guy walk into a radio studio …</p><p>That’s the state of Chicago sports radio, where the talent pipeline apparently has dried up, creating opportunities for radio neophytes to learn on the job.</p><p>How else to explain The Score’s forthcoming pairing of former WGN sports anchor Jarrett Payton with former reporter and columnist David Haugh on its morning show? <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/08/23/jarrett-payton-mike-mulligan-the-score-sports-radio-chicago-morning-show-david-haugh-walter-payton" >The station announced Monday</a> that Payton would replace the fired Mike Mulligan beginning next Monday.</p><p>Payton was at WGN for more than a decade and the defunct CLTV before that. He’s personable and charismatic, he’s well-liked and he’s the son of “Sweetness,” legendary Bears running back Walter Payton. No team in town moves the needle like the Bears. Payton could be a hit.</p><p>Or he could be hit, as in the ratings. Payton will move from half-hour TV shows to 4 ½-hour radio shows. Does he have enough opinions to fill that airtime? Will those opinions be critical of the Bears, particularly team ownership, which treats him like family? Can he speak with authority about the Cubs’ and White Sox’ playoff pushes? He’s entering a different world.</p><p>Haugh has been on The Score’s morning show since 2018, when previous management unceremoniously replaced Brian Hanley, who did nothing to deserve it. Yes, Hanley was a newspaper guy, too, but he excelled in radio, often carrying Mulligan. He had been at the station since its inception in 1992.</p><p>We might never know what hypnosis Haugh has performed on Chicago radio and TV executives. What we do know is that never before has someone who has said so little been given so much airtime to say it. In addition to mornings on The Score, he appears in the evening on Chicago Sports Network’s “The Chicago Lead” and “The Big Pro Football Show” because … well, he can.</p><p>Don’t get me wrong. Haugh is a nice enough guy. After years of criticizing his blandness and overexposure, I approached him at the Barrett Sports Media Summit when it was in town last year. I introduced myself and asked if there was anything he wanted to say to me, and he politely replied, “No.” I told him my criticism was purely professional, we chatted a bit and I went on my way.</p><p>I once wrote that Haugh used to write long for the Tribune, and now he talks long for The Score. The point still stands. He might have to talk even more — gasp! — until Payton gets his sea legs. There could be some rough waters in the beginning. The most opinionated person on the show is executive producer Dustin Rhoades. That’s a problem.</p><p>While Haugh helps hone Payton — gasp! — Payton will try to bring more out of Haugh. A personality, perhaps. A veteran of the radio business once asked me what I knew about Haugh off the air. My answer: very little. The vet said that’s an issue because it can prevent a connection with listeners. Even for sports-talk hosts, sports only go so far.</p><p>Payton isn’t shy talking about himself, his family, his kids and his father. Will he be able to draw more out of Haugh on a personal level? If the last eight years are any indication, he might need a power tool to drill deep enough.</p><p>Haugh has done what he was hired to do: play the hits. In other words, stick to sports. That was management’s mantra when Haugh arrived, as the sports landscape became overwhelmed with political and social issues. Maybe it’s just not in his nature to talk about himself.</p><p>Which begs the question: Why not replace “Mully and Haugh” completely? The Score made the right move in finally ending Mulligan’s reign of revolting radio – meandering questions, unfinished thoughts, inaudible words. Why not blow it up and start over?</p><p>According to sources, The Score contacted former host Danny Parkins, who now appears on FS1’s “First Things First.” Parkins left the station on good terms and is still connected through his annual radiothon for brain-cancer research. But the sides never came close.</p><p>That speaks to the dried-up pipeline at The Score, which in the last few years lost Parkins, fired Dan Bernstein and wasn’t able to bring back Jason Goff, a homegrown talent also needlessly let go by previous management. Goff worked his way up as a producer, earning prime hosting jobs. Who’s the next to follow that path?</p><p>We’re entering a fantastic time in Chicago sports. The Bears are a hot team nationally, the Cubs and Sox are on track to make the playoffs, Patrick Kane is back with the Blackhawks and the Bulls might have a star in Caleb Wilson. There’s a ton to talk about.</p><p>Are the best people in place to do the talking?<br></p>

entries.title: Krishnamoorthi wants U.S. to adopt wartime lessons from Ukraine, including drone usage
entries.summary: <p>Fresh off a 10-day congressional delegation trip to five European countries, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi thinks the U.S. should be taking notes from Ukraine when it comes to their battlefield tactics, including how the widespread usage of drones is changing warfare.</p><p>Krishnamoorthi traveled to Europe on Aug. 10 for an official trip focused on national security, intelligence, transatlantic cooperation and shared security challenges — with stops in Italy, Ukraine, Finland, Sweden and Norway. </p><p>In Kyiv, Krishnamoorthi met with embassy officials to discuss the battlefield situation as Ukraine enters year five of Russian attacks. The congressman also visited a Ukrainian drone-defense production site — a stop that inspired him to introduce the LESSONS from Ukraine Act, which would require the Pentagon to study how Ukraine has adapted to the use of drones, including the use of unmanned systems for combat, intelligence and logistics. Krishnamoorthi wants the Pentagon to also assess how drones are changing the survivability of armored vehicles and battlefield medicine, and develop a plan for incorporating lessons into U.S military training.</p><p>“We have got to increase our use of drones for reconnaissance, but also for attack purposes,” Krishnamoorthi told the Sun-Times. “...And also, think about how drones are going to render less important the use of tanks, armored vehicles, and stationary attack systems now compared to before… We have to learn from the Ukrainians about how to defeat drone attacks.”</p><p>Krishnamoorthi, who serves as a senior member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, said the U.S. must also make weapons "more resilient, faster and cheaper." And he thinks the country should also be viewing warfare from a standpoint of “deterrence.”</p><p>“We never want to go to war. We never want a conflict. We want to prevent it. But right now, i don’t think that we are well positioned to prevent conflict,” said Krishnamoorthi, who has been a vocal critic of the Iran war. “In fact, I fear that we’re sliding toward it, in part because of what’s happening in Iran.”</p><p>Krishnamoorthi said Ukraine is almost out of PAC-3 interceptors — interceptors designed to destroy missiles and aircraft— and he wants the U.S. to adopt a strategy to phase in the co-development of the systems, either in Ukraine or in allied countries. </p><p>"Because if we don't, I fear that a lot of Ukrainian targets are going to be sitting ducks for the Russians, especially as we approach the winter and they'll be in a more vulnerable position," Krishnamoorthi said. </p><p>The congressman said he also got a firsthand look at how Ukrainians are suffering, including families sheltering in their bathtubs to hide from danger.</p><p>“It’s really rough… Tens of thousands of Ukrainians shelter in the subways underneath the city. I think one day they counted 40,000 people who actually stayed overnight in those subways because of the relentless attacks by the Russians that day,” Krishnamoorthi said. “And this takes an incredible toll on families. Not to mention the fact that you have upwards of a million men who’ve been taken away from their families… The toll on Ukrainians can’t be overstated. But at the same time, they are some of the bravest people I’ve met.”</p><p>In Finland, Krishnamoorthi met with U.S. and Finnish officials and security partners about deterrence efforts against Russia. And in Sweden, the congressman met with Swedish partners to discuss security and defense cooperation. In Norway, Krishnamoorthi met with U.S. and Norwegian officials about Arctic and Baltic security, naval operations and efforts to counter Russian activity in the region.</p><p>Krishanmoorthi’s Italy trip included a visit to the Vatican to meet Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV, where he heard tales of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/08/21/pope-leo-xiv-white-sox-pope-hat-game-us-rep-raja-krishnamoorthi-visit" target="_blank" >pope’s allegiance to the Chicago White Sox</a> — and the congressman gifted him a jersey from the Cubs. </p>

entries.title: CBP agent says feds' 'Broadview 6' misconduct tainted his sexual assault case
entries.summary: <p>A U.S. Customs and Border Protection<b> </b>officer<b> </b>who allegedly<b> </b>used his gun and badge<b> </b>to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >rape multiple women</a><b> </b>is asking a judge<b> </b>to toss his indictment<b> </b>because it was returned<b> </b>by the same grand jury allegedly<b> </b>“indoctrinated”<b> </b>through the feds’ misconduct<b> </b>in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six” case</a>.</p><p>Not only that, but a key witness<b> </b>against<b> </b>Luis<b> </b>Uribe<b> </b>testified<b> </b>before the grand jury<b> </b>the same day some of the alleged “Broadview Six” misconduct<b> </b>occurred, according to defense attorney Michael<b> </b>Clancy.</p><p>However, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/22/broadview-six-damage-spreads-boutros-drops-more-charges-details-ongoing-review" target="_blank" >the veteran prosecutor</a> at the center of the “Broadview Six” controversy did not handle the case against Uribe, who faces trial Sept. 8 on charges contained in an<b> </b>11-count<b> </b>indictment<b> </b>handed up in December.</p><p>Federal prosecutors say Uribe<b> </b>committed<b> </b>multiple<b> </b>“gunpoint sexual assaults”<b> </b>of four women<b> </b>in Schaumburg and Naperville<b> </b>between February and October 2022. He’s been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/12/15/border-protection-officer-to-be-held-in-custody-while-awaiting-trial-on-sexual-assault-claims" target="_blank" >held in federal custody</a> since<b> </b>his Dec. 9 arrest, records show.</p><p>Clancy on Monday asked<b> </b>U.S. District Judge<b> </b>Jorge<b> </b>Alonso<b> </b>to dismiss the indictment against Uribe. In the alternative, Clancy asked the judge to hold a hearing<b> </b>and order prosecutors<b> </b>to hand over grand jury materials.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" >O’Hare-based Border Protection officer sexually abused, robbed women at gunpoint, indictment claims</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Alonso could take up the request Wednesday, when a pretrial conference is set to take place. The feds have yet to respond directly to Clancy’s request.</p><p>After a similar challenge was made in a separate case<b> </b>last month, prosecutors told a judge there was no reason to believe one prosecutor’s misconduct “so infected other grand jury sessions to render them void.”</p><p>Still, 10 people in three cases<b> </b>have seen their charges dropped<b> </b>as a result of the apparent misconduct uncovered in the “Broadview Six” case — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >the collapsed prosecution</a> of six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" >U.S. District Judge<b> </b>April Perry</a><b> </b>has yet to rule on<b> </b>a bid for sanctions<b> </b>or a special counsel<b> </b>in that case. Clancy argued Monday that the full extent of misconduct<b> </b>by the veteran prosecutor at the center of the controversy “will never be known without discovery and an evidentiary hearing.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" >‘Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The prosecutor in question is Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg who, on Oct. 9, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/09/broadview-six-grand-jury-midway-blitz-boutros-trump" target="_blank" >allegedly engaged in a forbidden practice</a> in the “Broadview Six” case known as “vouching.”</p><p>It’s improper, and it occurs when a prosecutor puts her personal credibility on the line to push for criminal charges.</p><p>Mecklenburg told the panel, “I want to go in front of the Thursday grand jury because I know you and I trust you and you know me and you trust me, and I would never ask you to charge somebody if I didn’t think there was probable cause and you know you’ve asked me before, ‘Well, what about this person?’ And I said, ‘I don’t charge people unless I’m absolutely sure.’”</p><p>That left the grand jury “hopelessly tainted,”<b> </b>Clancy argued.</p><p>Meanwhile, the defense attorney pointed to other “possible misconduct”<b> </b>— or “at the very least irregularities”<b> </b>— that occurred the same day<b> </b>as Mecklenburg’s alleged misconduct.</p><p>An alleged victim in Uribe’s case<b> </b>testified<b> </b>before the same grand jury<b> </b>with help from a Mandarin<b> </b>interpreter, Clancy wrote. At some point, prosecutors decided<b> </b>the interpreter’s translation was inaccurate.</p><p>There’s an audio recording of the testimony, Clancy wrote, but no<b> </b>official<b> </b>court<b> </b>reporter’s<b> </b>transcript. Instead, prosecutors turned over “a later FBI translation and transcript that the United States Attorney’s Office has deemed accurate,”<b> </b>Clancy said.</p><p>“Thus, on Oct. 9, 2025, on the same afternoon that [Mecklenburg] egregiously indoctrinated the Special June 2024 grand jury, that same grand jury also heard mistranslated questions and answers by [the alleged victim] in Uribe’s case,” Clancy wrote.</p><p>“The later FBI translation and transcript do not cure the gross error of the grand jury receiving mistranslated testimony."</p>

entries.title: Indiana governor directs state to investigate NIPSCO as power outages last nearly 2 weeks
entries.summary: <p>Indiana Gov. Mike Braun is calling for an investigation into the utility provider for Northwest Indiana as thousands remain without power in the area. </p><p>Braun directed the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor to file a complaint against NIPSCO with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, which regulates the state's utility companies. </p><p>Power has remained out for thousands of Northwest Indiana residents since the Aug. 11 storms that wrecked havoc on the state. The combination of 99-mph winds and flooding caused trees to topple over onto power lines, homes and onto roads.</p><p>Braun called for a thorough review of NIPSCO's preparedness for storm damage, including whether the utility had adequately protected its infrastructure and had been keeping vegetation cleared near its power lines. </p><p>NIPSCO issued a statement Monday saying it was aware of Braun's directive and "will cooperate fully if the Commission were to open an investigation."</p><p>The statement continued: "Throughout this event, our focus has remained on safely restoring service, supporting impacted communities and helping customers recover. As restoration efforts continue, our crews, contractors and partners remain committed to restoring power safely and as quickly as possible for every customer affected by this historic storm."</p><p>The utility has roughly 500,000 customers in northern Indiana and, according to the utility, about 374,500 of them lost power due to the storm. As of Monday morning, most of the customers who lost power during the storm had their lights back on. But about 10,000 customers still didn't have power, the vast majority of whom live in Gary. The city suffered the largest power outage of the region. NIPSCO estimates power will be back on for remaining customers as of Tuesday evening. </p><p>“NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes. NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain," Braun said in a statement. </p><p>On Sunday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/23/lawsuit-nipsco-neglected-power-lines-hazard-trees-storms-northwest-indiana-weather-electricity" target="_blank" >Braun said in social media post</a> that NIPSCO has “no excuse for these delays” after he sent teams from the Indiana National Guard, Indiana State Police and state natural resources and corrections departments to “literally clear the way for NIPSCO utility crews.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/23/lawsuit-nipsco-neglected-power-lines-hazard-trees-storms-northwest-indiana-weather-electricity" target="_blank" >A class-action lawsuit</a> representing several Northwest Indiana residents also claimed the utility did not protect its power lines from tree damage ahead of the storms.</p><p>The complaint, filed last Monday in Porter County, Indiana, claims NIPSCO failed to remove “hazardous trees and other vegetation” near power lines, neglected to conduct regular pole and line inspections, and ignored residents’ requests for vegetation management.</p>
