entries.title: Inside the long battle between Bears RT Darnell Wright and DE Montez Sweat that brought the best out of both
entries.summary: <p>Darnell Wright makes it look easy, and it’s hard to imagine this now that he’s one of the NFL’s best right tackles, but not that long ago he ran into something he couldn’t handle.</p><p>Early in his rookie season with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> in 2023, Wright wasn’t ready for Montez Sweat, then with the Commanders. On the Bears’ opening possession, Sweat went straight at Wright, pushed him back a step, then raced past him to take down Justin Fields.</p><p>Sweat was overwhelming. Little did Wright know, he'd soon become a daily problem for him.</p><p>A month later, with Wright still smarting from that sack, the Bears <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/08/26/de-montez-sweat-says-getting-traded-to-bears-definitely-worked-out-as-he-eyes-monster-season" >traded a second-round pick for Sweat</a> and began a yearslong battle on the practice field. Those two go against each other on nearly every rep, and it took a while, but it tilted from Sweat kicking Wright’s butt to him admitting that Wright currently has his number.</p><p>“He’s made me tremendously better,” Wright told the Sun-Times. “He’s the perfect body style for a player I want to go against: long and lanky. That’s the kind of guy I’ll struggle with sometimes.</p><p>“He has everything. He’s my litmus test for a lot of things. Going up against him gets me prepared to face elite guys.”</p><p>Their matchups have become must-watch in practice, and linebacker T.J. Edwards called it a collision of “two freaks of nature” with Wright standing 6-foot-5, 325 pounds and the ultra-athletic Sweat attacking him full-force at 6-foot-6, 270.</p><p>Neither is much of a talker, especially Wright, so their battles are quiet aside from the crash of pads and some grunting, but they’ll have a significant say in how far the Bears go.</p><p>Wright is essential to protecting quarterback Caleb Williams and powering what coach Ben Johnson has called a “righthanded offense” because that side of the line with Wright and guard Jonah Jackson is so strong. He called Wright “a luxury” who can “carry the load” in the running game if needed. Sweat is coming off what Johnson thought was his best season and is by far the most firepower the Bears have in their pass rush.</p><p>Between the two, the Bears have invested nearly a quarter of a billion dollars, with Wright fresh off signing a $116 million contract extension that made him the highest-paid right tackle of all time.</p><p>They’ve gotten a good return on each of them. Wright allowed just three sacks last season, while Sweat has had 21 1/2 sacks in 42 games and been very good against the run. The Bears need both to be elite this season as they rework their offensive line and hope something finally sparks their pass rush.</p><p>Sweat has felt their competition shifting over the years. He described the rookie version of Wright as an impressive, but unrefined talent who still had a lot to learn about dealing with standout pass rushers.</p><p>It evened out, in his view, last season as their reps became “hit for hit,” and Wright was good enough to earn a second-team All-Pro selection. He made things much easier for Williams with a 95.2% win rate on pass blocks, fourth in the NFL.</p><p>That still wasn’t the best Wright could do.</p><p>“This year I just see a huge jump in his technique,” Sweat marveled.</p><p>That put Wright on top.</p><p>“I don’t think I’ve beaten him in a one-on-one rep yet,” Sweat said of this training camp. “It started off with me making him better, but now I think it’s the other way around.”</p><p>Wright pushed back on that.</p><p>“He’s probably putting a little extra on there,” he said with a smile. “He’s definitely won some reps against me.”</p><p>That humility is part of the charm with Wright. It’s genuine from someone who has never appeared to seek the spotlight.</p><p>When the Bears drafted Wright 10th overall, he bypassed attending the draft and walking on stage in favor of enjoying it with family and friends. He’s friendly and available to reporters, but never eager.</p><p>He seemed reluctant a few weeks ago to do a news conference about his new nine-figure deal. Some players wear suits and bring their families to such an occasion. Wright came in after practice wearing a gray Bears workout shirt, thanked Jesus, said the money “doesn’t get me into Heaven” and went through a list of coaches and other people who helped him get here.</p><p>That’s largely how he approaches his job, too. Even after Sweat himself said it, Wright didn’t believe he had taken over their rivalry.</p><p>“You never think you’ve caught up or you’ve gotten where you need to be,” he said. “There’s always good reps and bad reps. I don’t keep count. Just trying my best.”</p><p>The Bears can’t wait to see how good Wright’s best ultimately is. He just turned 25, is only beginning his prime and is under contract through 2031. He should be a pillar of their future, and they can thank Sweat for pushing him to the next level.</p>

entries.title: Review: Usher and Chris Brown solidify why they are still the torchbearers of modern R&B despite controversy
entries.summary: <p>Usher and Chris Brown are two generational titans from two overlapping eras of R&B and pop music. Seeing them share a stage for “The R&B Tour” (a play on their last names) at a sold-out Soldier Field on Friday felt like seeing the last of a dying breed: male superstars who turn their passionate vulnerability into the highest forms of divine, musical masculinity.</p><p>The singers delivered a well-orchestrated, collaborative show. They were in sync from the moment Breezy arrived on stage in a stylish Canadian tuxedo and a Cubs hat, with Usher coming right after in an all-red leather outfit to perform “Party” together. And the beauty of the tour was how seamlessly their styles blended. Usher recreated the vibes from his Vegas residency times 10 while Brown gave fans an experience like they were at the UniverSoul Circus.</p><p>Twenty-one years ago, when Brown arrived with his self-titled debut, he quickly became the golden boy of R&B and pop. The album went 4x platinum, making it one of the most successful debut albums of his generation. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/42c2ec1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6643x3728+0+351/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F49%2F8b%2F5cf7e0494ec79de6f17ebeae215b%2Fusherchrisbrown-260824-13.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/37d1cfc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6643x3728+0+351/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F49%2F8b%2F5cf7e0494ec79de6f17ebeae215b%2Fusherchrisbrown-260824-13.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/42c2ec1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6643x3728+0+351/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F49%2F8b%2F5cf7e0494ec79de6f17ebeae215b%2Fusherchrisbrown-260824-13.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Usher performs Friday during The R&B Tour at Soldier Field.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“... I suspect that the unconscious distancing between art and artist that I experienced is far more common than a deliberate sequestration of the two. It’s also easier. And while that may aid a superficial kind of enjoyment, it inhibits a deeper understanding of the work and its significance. Such is the power — and danger — of performance,” writes Seletsky.</p><p>This is why nostalgia is so powerful in music. Fans pack stadiums for these tours because they want to relive the songs from the prime of their youth. Usher stuck to the hits, and while Breezy did the same, he also performed some more recent songs like the bluesy “Fallin’” where he came out atop an old-school Chevy Impala. The energy level was high as Gen X and millennial fans passionately sang the lyrics to Usher’s sultry “Nice & Slow” word for word as he teased the crowd by seductively trailing his fingers down his bare chest and abs, and down his pants when he sung, “I got plans to put my hands in places/I never seen, girl, you know what I mean.” Same for songs like Brown’s “Poppin’” and “Run It,” two songs from his debut album, that soundtracked high school parties across Chicago.</p><p>Despite addressing the ongoing criticism for his actions on “Leave Me Alone” from his latest album “BROWN,” he's avoided it on “The R&B Tour.” He and Usher have focused more on creating a joyous atmosphere for an intergenerational love fest. Fans were brought back to a time when men sang to women outside in the rain and yearned for a woman’s love (which special guest Tank surprisingly did to “I Deserve”). <b></b></p><p>Usher and Brown’s “The R&B Tour” is one of the best showcases of Black music this year and will be remembered for years to come. entries.title: Zillow resolves FTC lawsuit over claims it paid Redfin to suppress rental listings
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has reached a settlement with Zillow and Redfin to resolve the regulator's claim that the companies made an illegal deal to suppress competition in online rental advertising.</p><p>The FTC said Monday that it filed a proposed order with the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. It essentially requires Redfin to restart its standalone rental housing listings business, which the commission says will restore competition in the market for rental property listings. The settlement also resolves litigation brought by state attorneys general in Arizona, Connecticut, New York, Virginia and Washington.</p><p>“This settlement delivers better, quicker, more certain results for both renters and property management companies than we would have been able to achieve after prevailing at trial, including firm and enforceable commitments by Redfin to relaunch its rentals advertising business,” Daniel Guarnera, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Competition, said in a statement.</p><p>In its complaint filed almost a year ago, the FTC claimed that in exchange for $100 million and other compensation from Zillow, Redfin had agreed to shut down its internet listings and exclusively repost Zillow's apartment listings, transition its customers to Zillow and stay out of the apartment listings market for up to nine years.</p><p>The commission argued that the companies’ February 2025 pact violated federal antitrust laws and could reduce incentives for competition, leading to higher prices and fewer choices for multifamily rental advertising customers.</p><p>Zillow and Redfin said their agreement was not anticompetitive and benefited renters and property managers alike.</p><p>The FTC’s proposed order requires Redfin to restart its rental listings business and hire enough staff to maintain it within six months of the order being finalized, or face financial penalties. The FTC said Redfin fired hundreds of employees shortly after announcing its deal with Zillow.</p><p>And while Redfin will continue to syndicate Zillow’s listings, it will be free to seek out and advertise non-Zillow listings, according to the FTC.</p><p>In a statement Monday, Seattle-based Zillow said it “has consistently maintained the partnership with Redfin is pro-consumer and procompetitive, and we’re pleased to have found a resolution that enables its continuation.”</p><p>A spokesperson for Redfin, which was acquired by Detroit-based mortgage giant Rocket Companies last year, said Monday that the agreement “allows us to maintain our rental partnership with Zillow through at least 2030 while building and investing in a standalone rentals business of our own.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/22/chicago-area-homes-back-zillow-mred-federal-court-partial-victory" >Chicago-area homes back on Zillow after partial court victory</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/20/zillow-trulia-mred-listings-pln-chicago-vanished" >Thousands of Zillow listings in Chicago have vanished. entries.title: Crowd gathers after I-55 crash reportedly caused by federal immigration agents
entries.summary: <p>Federal immigration agents crashed into a truck on I-55 before chasing and detaining a man in McKinley Park Monday, drawing a crowd of protesters who remained on scene for hours after, according to Ald. Julia Ramirez (12th).</p><p>Ramirez said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents pinned a pickup truck on the highway before chasing a man and detaining him. Her office was asking anyone who may have knew him to reach out.</p><p>Illinois State Police, in a statement, did not mention a chase but confirmed deputies responded to a two-vehicle crash involving ICE agents near the I-55 northbound ramp to Damen Avenue around noon. They said no one was injured.</p><p>About a dozen federal vehicles arrived on scene in the 3300 block of South Wolcott Avenue with agents, as some taunted residents, who shouted back “get out of our city” and blew whistles.</p><p>It was unclear why agents arrested the man. However, a reporter heard an ICE officer at the scene tell protesters that the person arrested had a prior DUI.</p><p>A Chicago police commander could be seen speaking on the phone nearby after officers arrived around 2 p.m. as several residents stood within feet of the agents. Other residents stood behind the fence of the Target parking lot where the truck had been moved.</p><p>Ramirez said the situation brought to mind the lead up and aftermath of when Border Patrol agent Charles Exum <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >shot Marimar Martinez</a> two miles southwest of Monday's scene in Brighton Park on Oct. 4, 2025.</p><p>“This reminds me of the scene when Marimar was shot,” Ramirez said. “ICE agents escalated the situation, they came to safeguard the vehicle. I worry about a lot of people coming to the scene and them wanting to hurt people with pepper balls and tear gas.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Second man dies after Chicago Lawn shooting
entries.summary: <p>A second man has died after an early Sunday shooting in the Chicago Lawn neighborhood, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Darwin Cohone, 27, and Miguel Pinto Garcia, 29, were found on the ground around 5:45 a.m. in the 6100 block of South Campbell Avenue, police said. </p><p>Garcia, shot in the head, was pronounced dead at the scene while Cohone suffering from multiple gunshots to his torso, was taken in critical condition to Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn, where he died, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>No additional details were immediately available.<br></p>

entries.title: Were the preseason rankings wrong? Breaking down some major developments from Week 1 of high school football
entries.summary: <p>Top-ranked Mount Carmel, No. 2 Brother Rice and No. 5 Nazareth all lost in Week 1. Does that mean the preseason rankings were lousy?</p><p>The Caravan’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/22/mount-carmel-football-east-st-louis" >loss to East St. Louis</a> wasn’t a major surprise, despite the team's college talent and four consecutive state championships. East St. Louis is nearly as loaded with college talent and, most importantly, returned starting quarterback Reece Shanklin.</p><p>That was the common thread (and the possible weakness) among all three top teams that picked up opening-week losses: quarterback questions.</p><p>Shanklin was excellent for the Flyers, playing nearly perfectly other than one interception in the end zone. Mount Carmel is clearly still working out its quarterback situation. Brother Rice is starting an inexperienced senior and a star freshman, and Nazareth has a junior transfer quarterback from Wisconsin.</p><p>The best of that bunch so far is Nazareth’s JJ Chapman. He holds multiple Power Four offers and threw for 292 yards with one TD and two interceptions in the Roadrunners’ loss at IC Catholic.</p><p>One thing to keep in mind about the preseason rankings: they are based on what will likely happen throughout the season. Obviously, things can be rough for teams, even very talented ones, that don’t have the quarterback position settled. That wasn’t a huge surprise.</p><p>It is still very likely that Mount Carmel (8A), Brother Rice (7A) and Nazareth (6A) will win state titles this season and wind up at the top of the final Super 25.</p><h3>Eye openers</h3><p>Highly-ranked teams losing big games took everyone’s attention away from some other very interesting results.</p><p>Three teams that nearly made the preseason Super 25 picked up losses to good teams that are better than expected.</p><p>St. Laurence, which has done nothing but win and advance deep into the playoffs the past three seasons, lost 15-14 to King. The Jaguars were 7-5 with a young team last season and appear to be nearing the top tier of Public League football. They have a huge test at Marist this week.</p><p>DePaul Prep, which had multiple key players transfer away after coach Mike Passarella left for a college job, knocked off Richards 32-22 on the road. Junior running back Tyson Hooks finished with 190 yards and 2 TDs. Nick Bizzieri, previously the offensive line coach, is the new head coach.</p><p>Fremd returned a small core from last season’s excellent team, but some road bumps were possible after quarterback Johnny O’Brien left for Northwestern. Meanwhile, the arrow was pointing way up for Lake Zurich, which nearly cracked the preseason rankings.</p><p>The Vikings dominated with a 20-0 win on Friday, led by their defense. Junior Will Clark stepped in at quarterback and threw for 213 yards.</p><h3>Public League progress?</h3><p>King’s win against St. Laurence was the highlight of the week for the Public League. Simeon lost 44-28 at Marist. That game wasn’t as close as expected.</p><p>Morgan Park, talented but very young this season, lost to ranked Downers Grove North 17-12, and Kenwood lost to a good Palatine team 20-18.</p><p>Morgan Park coach Chris James and Kenwood’s Chris Goffer aren’t satisfied with moral victories at this point, but those close scores indicate both teams can strive towards significant playoff runs this season.</p><p>Remember, just as with Mount Carmel and Brother Rice, it isn’t the Week 1 result that matters. It is where a team finishes in November.</p>

entries.title: Former Bears WR Allen Robinson officially retires
entries.summary: <p>Allen Robinson, who had 3,561 receiving yards from 2018-21 with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, officially retired Monday.</p><p>In a nine-minute video he posted to social media, Robinson detailed the stops in his career, starting with youth football. He said it was “always special to me” to compete against the Packers and Aaron Rodgers, saying he swapped jerseys with the quarterback after one of their rivalry games. </p><p>He last played in an NFL game two years ago, with his hometown Lions. He said he felt his body “slowing up” and appreciated that his career was able to come full circle.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">With gratitude 🙏🏾 <a href="https://t.co/bGQXhivk7e">https://t.co/bGQXhivk7e</a></p>— Allen Robinson II (@AllenRobinson) <a href="https://x.com/AllenRobinson/status/2092026532105470363?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Robinson signed with the Bears as a free agent before their magical 2018 season. He led the team in receiving with 754 yards. He had 1,147 and 1,250, respectively, the following two seasons. Robinson entered the 2020 season eager to sign a contract extension, but the Bears eventually gave him the franchise tag for the following season before he left for free agency. He has the 11th-most receiving yards in Bears history.</p><p>Robinson had one-year stints with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2022/3/17/22977579/allen-robinson-contract-free-agent-guaranteed-chicago-bears-stats-quarterbacks-salary" target="_blank" >Rams</a>, Steelers and Lions. A second-round pick out of Penn State, Robinson's only Pro Bowl season came in his second year with the Jaguars, when he had a whopping 1,400 receiving yards.<br></p>

entries.title: As Trump pushes sweeping changes to mail voting, here's where things stand in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>As President Donald Trump continues to challenge mail ballots and push for a nationwide eligible registry list, many voters are confused about their own rights in the November midterm elections.</p><p>Trump in late July asked the U.S. Supreme Court to halt lower court decisions that blocked a March executive order that would make the federal government create a list of eligible voters and then require the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots specifically to those on the list. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/24/supreme-court-trump-administration-mail-voting-restrictions-ruling-midterms" >Supreme Court on Monday</a> froze a lower court’s ruling that had halted the order, but there’s another injunction that is still blocking the order.</p><p>Additional court challenges may also slow down the decision. Trump also wants the federal government to investigate and prosecute officials who issue ballots to “noncitizens.” The executive order came amid the president’s claims that people who lack legal status are voting.</p><p></p><p>Trump also is pushing Congress to pass his proposed Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, dubbed the SAVE Act, which would require proof of citizenship to vote. But his efforts have repeatedly stalled in the Senate.</p><p>Despite his ongoing fight against mail-in voting. Trump voted by mail once again in Florida's Republican primary. He also voted by mail in a special election in Palm Beach County earlier this year.</p><p></p><p>Here’s where things stand 10 weeks before Election Day.</p><h3><b>Can I vote if I live abroad?</b></h3><p>Illinois citizens who live overseas or are serving in the U.S. armed forces can register and vote by mail. Military personnel are allowed to register to vote and apply for a vote-by-mail ballot at the same time under Illinois law. The Federal Post Card Application is provided by the Defense Department to let members of the armed forces, their dependents and U.S. citizens abroad vote by mail, and if necessary, to register to vote.</p><h3><b>Can I view my voter registration information online?</b></h3><p>Yes. The Illinois State Board of Elections has a <a class="Link" href="https://ova.elections.il.gov/RegistrationLookup.aspx" target="_blank" ><u>registration website</u></a> where you can look up your registry with simple information like your full name, date of birth, address and ZIP code. It also gives you the deadlines to register. Applications are now open to request a vote-by-mail ballot in Illinois, including an <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/vote-mail#cboe-vote-by-mail" target="_blank" >online application for those in Chicago.</a> All requests by mail must be made by Sept. 24. Voters also can request a mail ballot in person.</p><h3><b>Do I need a passport to prove I’m a citizen to vote?</b></h3><p>No. In Illinois, you need at least one form of ID that has your current address to be able to register to vote — but not to actually vote. That ID could include a driver's license, bank statement, lease, utility bill or state ID. The SAVE Act would require a passport, a certified birth certificate with a photo ID, a naturalization certificate or a Consular Report of Birth abroad to register to vote in person.</p><h3><b>Have people who lack legal status voted in Illinois?</b></h3><p>“Noncitizen” voting is extremely rare, according to the Illinois State Board of Elections. Since 1982, only 10 noncitizens have been confirmed to have voted in an Illinois election.</p><h3><b>What happens if someone lacking legal status tries to vote?</b></h3><p>Under the National Voter Registration Act, voters are not required to show proof of U.S. citizenship when they register to vote. Voters must attest, under penalty of perjury, that they are U.S. citizens when completing their voter registration applications.</p><p>Voter registration applications created by the Illinois State Board of Elections ask, “Are you a citizen of the United States?” Applicants also are required to certify the following: “The information I have provided is true to the best of my knowledge under penalty of perjury. If I have provided false information, then I may be fined, imprisoned, or, if I am not a U.S. citizen, deported from or refused entry into the United States.” </p><p>Voters who register by other methods must also attest to their status as a citizen. If an applicant does not make the required certification of citizenship, the voter registration application will be denied.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c0304c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a96c6ec/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70ad95f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="People voting at George Rogers Clark Elementary School in Austin on March 17. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70ad95f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/54fdf7c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70ad95f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>People vote March 17 at George Rogers Clark Elementary School in Austin.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Should I turn in my mail ballot early in light of U.S. Postal Service changes? </b></h3><p>Yes. The Illinois State Board of Elections is recommending that voters mail back ballots as early as possible. To ensure that your mail ballot will be counted, it must be postmarked by Election Day and be received by the board of elections no later than 14 days after the date of the election. Under a new policy, mail is postmarked on the day it is processed at the post office, rather than on the day it is dropped in a mailbox.</p><h3><b>Is a ballot drop box secure?</b></h3><p>Not every election authority in Illinois has one, but, yes, according to the Illinois State Board of Elections, which has security measures in place for drop boxes. If your local election authority doesn’t have a drop box, you can hand-deliver your vote-by-mail ballot directly to election authorities.</p><h3><b>What happens if I didn’t get my mail ballot or I got it but want to vote in person instead?</b></h3><p>If you didn’t receive the mail ballot, you can go to your local election authority, fill out an affidavit attesting to the nonreceipt and vote with a regular ballot. If you got one and decided not to use it, you can surrender the vote-by-mail ballot to the election authority during early voting or on Election Day, and then vote in person<b>. </b></p><h3><b>Do I need a Real ID or a Social Security card to vote?</b></h3><p>No. You do not need to bring a Real ID or a Social Security card to vote.</p><h3><b>Do I need to have the name on my birth certificate as my voter registration name?</b></h3><p>No. But Trump’s SAVE Act would require you to bring in additional paperwork, such as a marriage certificate, if your name doesn’t match other IDs that you’ve brought. According to the nonpartisan website <a class="Link" href="http://vote.org" target="_blank" ><u>Vote.org</u></a>, an estimated 69 million American women do not have a birth certificate that matches their current legal name.</p><h3><b>Does the Justice Department have access to the Illinois voter registration database?</b></h3><p>No. But the Trump administration is trying to make that happen. The Illinois State Board of Elections is keeping track of litigation, which has seen a federal judge rule against giving that access. The Justice Department appealed the Illinois ruling in the voter roll case Aug. 17 in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/03/donald-trump-executive-order-national-voter-eligibility-list-mail-in-ballots-lawsuit-24-blue-states" >Illinois and other Democrat-led states sue against Trump executive order that tightens mail-in voting</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Supreme Court sides with Trump administration on mail voting restrictions ahead of midterms
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration Monday in a case over President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much can be implemented before the fast-approaching midterm elections.</p><p>The decision leaves room for additional court challenges that could further slow Trump's order, and other similar cases have already been filed. The U.S. Postal Service <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/postal-service-midterms-trump-mail-voting-b4b9ef095b4d6bceab18adbb34814640" target="_blank" >laid out how it would implement the order</a> last week, but time is running short to impose major changes with some states beginning to send mail ballots to voters in just a few weeks.</p><p>The Supreme Court's conservative majority didn’t decide the legality of Trump's order, instead ruling that the states did not have the legal right to challenge it.</p><p>“The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the majority wrote in an unsigned order.</p><p>The three liberal-leaning justices publicly dissented, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson writing that the rule “lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges.”</p><p>New York Attorney General Letitia James foreshadowed more legal wrangling, calling the decision a “painful setback” but vowing it would “not be the final word.”</p><p>The court’s order opens a path for the administration to begin action to restrict mail voting, but it also could lead to a bevy of potential further litigation that could freeze the federal government again, all starting 10 days before the first mail ballots in the nation are scheduled to be sent to overseas and military voters from North Carolina.</p><p>“This is just the first inning of a very fast nine-inning game,” said Derek Muller, a law professor at Notre Dame University.</p><h3>Trump fights mail-in voting despite its growing popularity</h3><p>Mail balloting has long been a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/f0a5b003db26dbb19778bcdcb45f9a3f" target="_blank" >favorite target</a> for Trump, who has claimed that it breeds fraud despite strong evidence to the contrary and his own use of <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-vote-by-mail-bd52fd205f4484237d5b77d2e7319350" target="_blank" >the voting method</a>.</p><p>Trump's executive order, signed in March, calls on his administration to create lists of eligible voters and orders the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists.</p><p>Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued to block the order. They argued that the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to run elections, and Trump’s changes could lead to chaos and partisan abuse.</p><p>“The consequences of allowing such transformative changes to take effect so close to this fall’s elections would be extreme,” attorneys for the states wrote. Dozens of state and local election officials weighed in, asking the justices to leave the order frozen while election preparations are already underway.</p><p>A judge in Massachusetts <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-appeal-executive-order-8bfb1f787f84fc60f9b6b284794b18b5" target="_blank" >blocked the plan</a> for the midterm elections in those states. An appeals court upheld her decision. She later granted a second order <a class="Link" href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/judge-again-bars-trump-administration-from-implementing-order-that-sought-to-limit-mail-voting/" target="_blank" >blocking it nationwide</a>, another potential stumbling block for Trump administration plan.</p><p>The Justice Department appealed to the Supreme Court on procedural grounds in late July, arguing that the states sued too soon. They also pointed to another ruling out of Washington, where a judge allowed Trump’s order to proceed. An appeals court backed that decision, while still leaving room for future court action if the changes are implemented.</p><p>Federal attorneys argued that the Massachusetts order “blocks the government’s ability to finalize and implement the President’s proposed policies to promote election integrity for the upcoming federal elections in November.”</p><p>A dozen Republican-leaning states supported the federal government in their own appeal before the high court, saying states would have input on the final voter lists.</p><p>The Supreme Court has previously ruled against Trump-backed arguments on mail-in ballots, finding in June that states can count ballots that arrive after Election Day. That case was decided after full briefing and arguments, rather than on the court’s emergency docket.</p><p>Trump has blamed mail voting — without credible evidence — for his loss to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. He has promoted the proposed changes in his executive order as safeguards to keep non-U.S. citizens from voting.</p><p>He’s also repeatedly pressed for the passage of the legislation that requires proof of citizenship to vote. Noncitizen voting has been shown to be rare, and is a felony that can be punishable by deportation.</p><p>Using mail ballots has become increasingly popular with voters of both parties, with about 30% of all ballots cast that way during the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. The process also is secure. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found only about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.</p>

entries.title: Daily Herald editorial staff announces unionization effort
entries.summary: <p>The editorial staff at suburban publication the Daily Herald has announced a unionization effort shortly after a wave of layoffs earlier this month, according to the Daily Herald News Guild.</p><p>It comes after 12 of the paper’s staffers were laid off, including executive editor Lisa Miner, the paper's copy desk and page designers, according to the guild. It’s the ninth time the staff has seen cuts since October 2017, with eight rounds of buyouts and three rounds of layoffs, including those in November 2024.</p><p>That cuts come as wages have been reduced by at least 15% and the work week cut to less than 37 hours over the last decade, the union said.</p><p>The guild has filed for a union election with the National Labor Relations Board, which means a formal vote to unionize has not yet been taken, but 19 of 20 eligible union members have signed cards in support of the union.</p><p>In a statement, the guild said it was created to “address high turnover, advocate for pay equity and strengthen the publication’s community-focused coverage.”</p><p>“For decades our newsroom has been decimated,” said Kevin Schmit, the Daily Herald’s associate sports editor and a 29-year employee. “And for too long crucial decisions have been made with no input from us, the editorial staff responsible for producing an award-winning newspaper. We take this step now to gain a seat at the table and because we remain committed to maintaining our status as the trusted voice of the Chicago suburbs.”</p><p>Tribune Publishing didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The Daily Herald was acquired by Tribune Publishing in June after the company ran a full-page ad in the Chicago Tribune offering a higher price than Shaw Media, which owns other suburban papers and had been in talks to make a purchase previously.</p><p>The paper has covered suburban Chicago since 1872, and was independently owned and run by the Paddock family for four generations. In 2018, the Paddock family members sold its portions of the company to its employees and set up an employee stock ownership plan.</p><p>But for the last several months, even prior to the acquisition, the guild had been in the process of unionizing, Schmit said.</p><p>“We’re motivated more than ever because of the layoffs,” Schmit told the Chicago Sun-Times. “[But] our union is a little smaller than it was two weeks ago.”</p><p>The Daily Herald News Guild is slated to join Chicago News Guild Local 34071 TNG-CWA, which represents more than 600 media, nonprofit and publishing workers throughout the Chicago area and nationally, including at the Sun-Times.</p><p>“Workers at the Daily Herald are ready to have a voice in their workplace and their futures,” said Chicago News Guild Local 34071 TNG-CWA President Owen Schmidt in a statement. “We’re looking forward to supporting these future members as they advocate for job security and to protect local news.”</p>
